title: Najdorf: the main line move by move, with reasons
outcomes: Steps through the 6.Bg5 e6 7.f4 Be7 line to move 15 and gives a reason for each move
Names the engine-checked alternative that fails at each key moment (6...b5, 8.Qe2, 10...O-O, 11.Kb1) and says what it forgets
Explains the pawn storm: g4, the trade on f6, g5 with tempo, f5, and Black's counter-play with ...b5 and ...b4
Reads opening counts with their sample sizes (948 games at move 6, 26 at move 12) and separates master from online data
Picks a plan when Black answers 6.Bg5 with the knight instead of ...e6: 7.Bc4, 7.Qe2 or 7.f4, with the counts for each

steps.caption: White to move, at the end of the line we study. Look at the kings and the pawns on f5 and g5. Which wing is White attacking? Write what you would aim at next, then watch how the position came about.

claims.statement: White's king stands on the queenside.
Black's king stands on the kingside.
The engine rates this position between +0.20 and +1.10 for White (depth 16).

steps.prompt: Before the moves: which side do you think stands better here, and what is your evidence on the board?

steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** A main line is a chain of choices. For each move we ask three things: what is it for, what does it cost, and which similar move fails? The line runs from the bishop's attack on the f6 knight, through the queen and long castling, to the pawn storm you just saw. By the end you can explain every move and name the trap beside it. Marks: [V] checked here, [I] inference, [H] hypothesis.

steps.caption: Moves 6 and 7. Step through them and say what each move leaves behind.

line.say: The bishop attacks the knight on f6, which guards e4 and d5. Cost: the bishop can be asked questions by ...h6 later.
Black frees the f8 bishop and guards d5. The pawn on e6 also takes f5 away from White.
The pawn takes e5 from Black, makes room for the queen on the third rank and for long castling.

claims.statement: Bg5, Be3 and f3 are all within 40 centipawns of the engine's best move (depth 16).
After Bg5 one white piece attacks the knight on f6.
After f4 one white pawn attacks e5.

steps.caption: A look-alike that fails. In many Najdorf lines Black pushes the b-pawn at once. Here the bishop on g5 is still pointed at f6, and the push leaves f6 with too little help.

line.say: The usual Najdorf pawn push, played without covering f6.
The queen joins the bishop in attacking f6. Black must now find a defence while the b-pawn has done nothing yet [I].

claims.statement: 6...b5 is at least 30 centipawns worse than the engine's best move (depth 16).
After 7.Qf3 two white pieces attack the knight on f6.

steps.caption: Why not take on f6 at once? The trade looks natural. Bxf6 is playable, about a tenth of a pawn behind f4 [V]. It hands Black a free queen development and gives up the bishop that prepares the storm, so the main line keeps the tension.

line.say: The bishop takes the knight, and Black's queen can recapture.
The queen recaptures with a developing move: Black's pawns stay intact and the queen eyes b2 and d4 [I].

claims.statement: f4 is within 40 centipawns of the engine's best move (depth 16); the trade on f6 is not the engine's pick.
After the trade the engine rates the position between -0.60 and +0.20 for White (depth 16).

steps.text: **Move 7: four sound replies.** After the f-pawn move, the engine puts four black moves within about 10 centipawns of each other: ...Be7, ...h6, ...Nbd7 and ...Qb6 [V]. In our master file the most played is the queen sortie to b6, the *Poisoned Pawn* (244 of 695 games), then ...h6, ...Be7 and ...Nbd7. The Poisoned Pawn comes back in lessons 6 to 8. We follow ...Be7 for the clearest structure [I].

steps.caption: Black to move. Master games (both players 2500+): ...Qb6 244, ...h6 203, ...Be7 102, ...Nbd7 90 of 695. Online, 2100+ band (Lichess, September 2026, games that visited the position): ...Be7 271, ...Qb6 125, ...h6 72, ...Nbd7 78 of 600. The same position, two different crowds [V].

claims.statement: ...Be7, ...Nbd7, ...h6 and ...Qb6 are all within 40 centipawns of the engine's best move (depth 16).

steps.caption: The most played reply in master games, previewed only. Black takes the b2 pawn with the queen; this is the Poisoned Pawn, which comes back in lessons 6 to 8.

line.say: The queen attacks the knight on d4 and the pawn on b2.
The queen guards b2 for the moment and develops.
Black takes the pawn anyway.

steps.caption: The same preview, continued: the rook attacks the queen and the queen runs to a3.

line.say: The rook attacks the queen.
The queen runs to a3; White now has lines and tempo for the pieces.

claims.statement: After this line the engine rates the position between -0.30 and +1.20 for White (depth 16).

steps.caption: Another sound reply (203 master positions): the h-pawn asks the bishop a question at once. The bishop must retreat or trade; the diagonal to f6 stays open for it.

line.say: The pawn attacks the bishop on g5.
The bishop retreats and keeps the knight on f6 in its sights.

claims.statement: After ...h6 one black pawn attacks the bishop on g5.

steps.caption: Moves 7 to 9, with a reason each. Say the purpose aloud first, then read it.

line.say: Develops, prepares castling and defends f6 so that a trade on f6 can be met by a recapture.
The queen leaves d1 so the king can castle long, and covers g4 for the coming pawn.
The queen lines up on the half-open c-file against the knight on c3 and frees d8.

claims.statement: After ...Be7 two black pieces defend the knight on f6 (the bishop on e7 and the pawn on g7).
After 8.Qf3 one white piece covers g4, the square of the coming pawn push.
After ...Qc7 the queen attacks the knight on c3 down the half-open c-file.

steps.caption: Move 9: the king leaves the centre and the last minor piece develops.

line.say: The king leaves the centre for the wing away from the pawn storm, and the rook reaches the d-file.
The last minor piece develops, adds a defender to f6 and prepares ...b5.

claims.statement: After long castling White's king stands on the queenside.
After ...Nbd7 three black pieces defend the knight on f6.

steps.caption: Black to move at move 8. Why does the queen go first? [I] It lines up on the c-file, leaves d8 free, and keeps the knight on b8 flexible for d7 or c6.

claims.statement: ...Qc7 and ...Nbd7 are both within 40 centipawns of the engine's best move (depth 16).

steps.text: **Move 8 in the data.** Master games (329,379 in the file): ...Qc7 in 69 of 86, ...h6 in 17. Online, 2100+ band: ...Qc7 149 of 251, ...Nbd7 48, ...h6 28, ...O-O 22 [V]. Same idea, different crowd: both prefer the queen.

steps.caption: The other main idea at move 9: strike in the centre at once instead of castling. The engine rates both within 40 centipawns [V]. We follow long castling because it keeps the plan simple [I].

line.say: The pawn attacks e6 and cramps the black position at once.

claims.statement: After f5 one white pawn attacks e6.
Long castling and f5 are both within 40 centipawns of the engine's best move (depth 16).

steps.text: **The same question twice.** Black's king is on e8 and the pieces aimed at the kingside are already there: the bishop on g5, the pawn on f4, the queen on f3. [I] Castling short would place the king in front of them. The next two positions differ in White's ninth move: castle long, or develop the bishop to d3 and keep the king at home. Predict if that matters.

steps.caption: White to move at move 10. There is a quieter plan too: develop the bishop to d3 and wait. Both are sound [V]; the lesson follows the pawn storm because its idea is easier to name [I].

line.say: The bishop develops and eyes h7; the king stays on c1 and the storm can start later.

claims.statement: g4 and Bd3 are both within 40 centipawns of the engine's best move (depth 16).

steps.caption: Move 10. The storm starts. Step through the pawn push and Black's answer.

line.say: The pawn heads for g5 to attack the knight on f6; the queen on f3 and the pawn on f4 stand behind it.
Black starts the counter-attack on the king that went to c1: the pawn gains space and may attack the knight on c3 later.

claims.statement: After this line the engine rates the position between +0.20 and +0.90 for White (depth 16).

steps.caption: Move 11. White can trade the bishop for the knight now. Why? [I] The bishop on g5 is the only piece in the way of the g-pawn, and the knight on f6 is the defender the pawn wants to chase.

line.say: The bishop takes the knight, clearing g5 for the pawn.
The knight from d7 recaptures; this keeps the structure and leaves a knight on f6 for the pawn to attack.

claims.statement: 11.Kb1 is at least 35 centipawns worse than the engine's best move (depth 16).
After the trade on f6 the engine rates the position between +0.00 and +0.80 for White (depth 16).

steps.caption: Move 12. The pawn arrives with tempo. Step through it and look at where the knight can go.

line.say: The pawn attacks the knight; the knight must move and the bishop on e7 stands behind it.
The only good square: the knight guards e5 and f6 and keeps the queen's diagonal.

claims.statement: After g5 one white pawn attacks the knight on f6.
12.Kb1 is at least 50 centipawns worse than the engine's best move (depth 16).

steps.caption: Move 13. The second pawn joins in.

line.say: The pawn attacks e6 and cramps the knight on d7.

claims.statement: After f5 one white pawn attacks e6.

steps.caption: Black to move. A pawn is hanging on g5, and the bishop on e7 can take it with check. Castling first is the engine's choice [V]. Why is castling right now, when it was wrong at move 9? The bishop that stood on g5 is gone and the g-pawn has already arrived, so no attack is waiting for the king, and the knight on d7 stands in front of it [I].

line.say: Black castles at last; the pawn on g5 is not worth the time, and the engine rates the capture lower than castling.

claims.statement: 13...Bxg5+ is at least 20 centipawns worse than the engine's best move (depth 16).
After castling Black's king stands on the kingside.

steps.caption: Moves 14 and 15. White supports the g5 pawn with the rook, and Black strikes back at once.

line.say: The rook guards the pawn on g5 and lines up on the g-file.
The pawn attacks the knight on c3: Black's counter-blow.

steps.caption: The knight steps aside and Black blunts the centre: the centre is the next battleground.

line.say: The knight steps aside and heads for g3 or d4; it also guards the d4 knight.
Black blunts the knight on d4 and the f-pawn: the centre is the next battleground.

claims.statement: After this line the engine rates the position between +0.20 and +1.10 for White (depth 16).
After the line, a white rook stands on g1.

steps.caption: The plans after move 15, read from the pawns. White to move has the half-open d-file, space on the kingside and a pawn on g5. Black has the half-open c-file and the b-pawn forward. [I] White: bring the h-pawn up to support g6 or f6. Black: bishop to b7, a rook to c8, pressure on c2.

claims.statement: The d-file is half-open for White and the c-file half-open for Black.

steps.prompt: [H] The engine rates this position about half a pawn better for White, but only when White finds the right plan on each move. Do you think Black should avoid this line, or is a small plus for White an acceptable price for a safe structure? Say what evidence you would collect.

steps.caption: What the numbers say along this line (master file, both players 2500+, 2012-2026). After 6.Bg5 e6: 948 games. 7.f4: 711. ...Be7 was played 102 times and 96 of those games go on to a recorded next move; some games end at a position, so counts also fall for that reason [I]. After 8.Qf3: 86, then 8...Qc7 in 69. After 9.O-O-O Nbd7: 58. After 10.g4: 51, then 10...b5 in 33. After 12.g5 Nd7: 26 games, White 7 wins, 11 draws, Black 8 [V].
steps.chapter: What the numbers say, and where it goes wrong

steps.caption: Black's other reply to the bishop (592 of 1,584 master positions) leads away from this lesson's line. With the knight on d7 the structure differs: the e-pawn stays on e7 and f6 has three defenders, so the f4 storm does not follow automatically [I]. White's most played moves here in the master file: 7.Bc4 (253 games), 7.Qe2 (194), 7.f4 (72). Online, 2100+ band: 7.f4 117, 7.Bc4 52 [V].

claims.statement: Three black pieces defend the knight on f6 (the knight on d7 and the pawns on e7 and g7).

steps.caption: The most played plan in master games (253 games). The bishop aims at f7, and Black's usual answer, the queen to b6 (191 of 245), hits b2 and d4 at once [V].

line.say: The bishop eyes f7 and keeps the knight on d4 and the pawn on e4 supported.
The queen attacks the knight on d4 and the pawn on b2: White must answer both threats.

claims.statement: 7.Bc4 is within 40 centipawns of the engine's best move (depth 16).
After 7.Bc4 a white piece attacks f7.

steps.text: **A funnel, not a verdict.** The line starts with 948 games and ends with 26. At the end the result (7 White wins, 11 draws, 8 Black wins) says almost nothing about the position: with 26 games a handful of different players or one favourite line moves it a lot [I]. Online, in the 1100-1300 band the position after ...e6 occurred 14 times and 7.f4 followed once; across 1100-1500 it is 82 and 16, so most club players choose something else here [V]. Check the claim, not the crowd.

steps.prompt: White won 7 of the 26 games that reached 12...Nd7 and Black won 8. Does that mean Black is doing better in this line?

fields.label: My answer:
options: no, the sample is far too small to say

steps.caption: Common mistake 1: the wrong queen square. On e2 the queen blocks the bishop on f1, which then has no future diagonal.

line.say: The queen leaves d1 but not for the best square.
Black gets time for the counter-attack, and the engine now rates the position level or better for Black [V].

claims.statement: 8.Qe2 is at least 40 centipawns worse than the engine's best move (depth 16).
After this line the engine rates the position between -0.60 and +0.30 for White (depth 16).

steps.caption: Common mistake 2: castling into the storm. The king arrives in front of the very pieces the pawn push is meant to help.

line.say: The king goes to g8.
The bishop keeps the knight tied: if it moves, the bishop on h4 takes on e7 [I].

claims.statement: 10...O-O is at least 45 centipawns worse than the engine's best move (depth 16).

steps.caption: The bishop keeps the knight tied and the pawn arrives with the king behind it: Black's counter-attack is too slow [I].

line.say: Black counter-attacks.
The pawn attacks the knight on f6 and the king stands behind it.

claims.statement: After g5 one white pawn attacks the knight on f6.

steps.caption: Common mistake 3: a calm king move. It looks careful, but it lets Black's pawn strike with tempo.

line.say: A waiting move: it avoids checks on the diagonal, but it does not help the storm.
The pawn attacks the knight on c3 and White has lost a tempo: the g-pawn storm must wait.

claims.statement: After ...b4 one black pawn attacks the knight on c3.

steps.text: **Recap: what to remember.** The bishop on g5 attacks f6; the e-pawn answers; the f-pawn takes e5. Black develops the bishop to e7 and the queen to c7; White's queen goes to f3 and the king to c1. The storm is g4, a trade on f6, g5 with tempo, then f5. Black counters with the b-pawn. Early short castling, the queen on e2 and the king on b1 each fail for a named reason. Counts thin out to 26 games by move 12.

steps.prompt: Teach-back: explain to a beginner why White's bishop goes to g5 and what the pawn on f4 stops. Say when the plan works and when it does not (for example when Black answers with the knight), give one position a beginner could set up, and one mistake to avoid. Self-check afterwards: did you name a condition, give an example, and warn about one error?
